title: Scheduler core in Java
idea: The scheduler core is a priority queue of tasks plus one loop: while the head is due, take it out, run it, then finish, repeat or retry it.

analogy.text: An airport departure board. The next flight on the list boards first; a delayed flight gets a new time and moves down the list.
analogy.breaks: Flights do not return every hour; recurring tasks do.

points: `runDue` reads the clock once, then drains every task due by then.
A task leaves the heap before its fields change, then re-enters later.
Cancel only flips the status; the loop drops cancelled tasks when it polls them.
Failures retry at now plus backoff until attempts reach the policy's maximum.

steps.caption: Five tasks wait. Cleanup is already cancelled but stays in the heap: removal is lazy.
At t=0 only the heartbeat is due. It runs, then returns with its next time. t=500 repeats this.
At t=1000 cleanup reaches the head. The loop sees CANCELLED and drops it without running.
Charge-card wins the 1000 tie with priority 5. It throws, so it returns with run time 1100.
Send-report and the heartbeat run next. The report is one-shot, so it finishes.
At t=1100 the second attempt fails too. Backoff doubles, so the next try is at 1300.
At t=1300 the third attempt succeeds and the task leaves the queue for good.
Bad-export fails at 1500, 1700 and 1900 (due at 1600, run at the next tick). After three attempts it is FAILED.

code.title: The complete core
code.caption: One-shot, recurring, cancelled and failing tasks on a manual clock. Task fields are package-private here, so `Scheduler` requeues directly.

walk.text: Charge-card fails twice, heartbeat repeats every 500 ms, bad-export always fails.
Move the manual clock through fixed ticks, running due work at each.
The heap orders tasks; the map finds them by id.
Cancel flips the status only; no linear search through the heap.
Drain every due task, skipping cancelled ones as they surface.
On success, finish a one-shot task or requeue the next period.
On failure, give up at the limit or requeue after the backoff.

pitfalls: Never edit run time while a task is in the heap; poll, change, then add.
Decide what a recurring task does after a long pause: catch up or skip missed runs.
Reset attempts after a recurring success, or later failures retry less than intended.

quiz.q: What is the first line CoreScheduler prints for t=1000?
options: t=1000 charge-card #1 gateway timeout, retry at 1100
quiz.why: Cleanup is cancelled and skipped silently. Of the three due at 1000, charge-card has the highest priority, and its first call throws.

takeaway: Poll the due head, run it, then finish, repeat or retry.

starters: Why remove cancelled tasks lazily instead of calling queue.remove?
Should a fixed-rate task's next run come from its run time or from now?
How would runDue change if jobs ran on a thread pool?
